titulo.texto: Recreation of the Dolní Věstonice Burial

frase_gancho.texto: Three young people buried together on red earth, tens of thousands of years ago.

puente_narrativo.texto: From a tomb we move on to skulls: bones tell stories too. Look for the skull mural in this hall and compare their shapes, their teeth, and the traces of customs left by very different peoples.

guion_corto.texto: Three young people rest together on earth stained red. Someone laid them there more than twenty-five thousand years ago, in the Upper Paleolithic. This is a life-size re-creation of a burial from Dolní Věstonice, in Moravia, in the south of the present-day Czech Republic. They were people of our own species, Homo sapiens, who lived by hunting and gathering. They were approximately sixteen to twenty years old, and they were buried at the same time, with no signs of violent death. The bodies are covered in red ocher and adorned with pierced teeth. Specialists see in these details one of the earliest pieces of evidence in Europe of symbolic thought and of rituals for bidding farewell to the dead.

guion_largo.texto:
When you think of prehistory, you may imagine people who were only trying to survive. This burial tells a different story: more than twenty-five thousand years ago, in a village of mammoth hunters, someone took the time to say farewell to three young people with care.

What you see is a life-size re-creation of a tomb found in 1986 in Dolní Věstonice, in Moravia, in the south of the present-day Czech Republic. It was made with replicas of the skeletons, with stone tools and with animal teeth, on a bed of earth mixed with red ocher. The three bodies lie stretched out, one beside another, and they were buried at the same time; no signs of violent death were found. The people who buried them lived by hunting mammoths, and in camps of the region, huts were built with the bones of this animal. In the next hall you will see the hunters who pursued that same giant in the Americas.

Notice how they are arranged. One of them lies face down. Another rests his hand toward the pelvis of the young man in the center, who, according to studies, was placed first. And red ocher was spread over their heads, a natural pigment made from iron oxide. In many cultures, red was associated with blood and with life. You will see something similar in the Maya Hall, where the body of King [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal) was covered with cinnabar, another red powder.

The young man in the center holds a secret that came to light over the years. He had a malformation in his bones from birth, which curved his legs. Even so, he lived to become a young man, and specialists think his group must have cared for him. It is one of the oldest pieces of evidence that, even then, humans looked after those who needed help.

There is also a curious detail. For a long time, the young man in the center was believed to be a woman. In 2016, a DNA analysis indicated that all three were male, and that they were possibly related. Science sometimes corrects what seemed obvious.

The bodies wore ornaments made from pierced animal teeth, which were probably sewn onto clothing or headdresses. Imagine the work of piercing a tooth with stone tools, and think of how much these three young people mattered to those who bid them farewell. For specialists, the ocher and the ornaments are among the earliest evidence in Europe of symbolic thought: the idea that an object can mean something more than its use.

The site is famous for another reason. At Dolní Věstonice, a baked clay figurine of a woman was found, the “Venus of Dolní Věstonice,” one of the oldest ceramics known. In other words: those hunters were firing clay long before the farming villages you will see in the Preclassic Hall existed.

Look at this scene as a reminder. Long before cities and gods, there were already people who bid farewell to their own with care. And that custom, more than any pyramid, lets us recognize ourselves.

texto: Count the bodies and notice how they are arranged
Look for the red ocher on the earth and on the bodies
Find the ornaments made from teeth and the stone tools

texto.Culture: Homo sapiens, hunter-gatherers of the European Upper Paleolithic (Gravettian)
texto.Material: Museum re-creation as a 1:1 scale diorama with replicas of the three skeletons, ocher pigment, and necklaces of pierced teeth

texto.pregunta: Myth: Prehistoric humans buried their dead without ceremony, in simple pits.
texto.respuesta: Reality: This multiple burial, with red ocher and tooth ornaments, shows funerary rituals in the Upper Paleolithic.
